traditional_use: Classical use of bitter gourd fruit for prameha, the sugar-related disease group.
pros: Long traditional record for blood sugar; small human studies report lower glucose.
cons: Human studies are small and mixed; very bitter; can upset the stomach.
cautions: Adds to the sugar-lowering effect of diabetes medicines; watch for low-sugar symptoms.
source_note: PMID 15521566 (human NIDDM study of hypoglycemic effect alongside oral antidiabetic drugs); PMID 19904502

traditional_use: Classical use of gurmar leaf for prameha; the Hindi name means sugar destroyer.
pros: Strong traditional record; animal studies show lower glucose and better insulin response.
cons: Human evidence is limited; may blunt sweet taste; product strength varies.
cautions: Adds to sugar-lowering medicines, so low-sugar episodes are possible.

traditional_use: Traditional use of methi seed for prameha and for digestion.
pros: Widely used as food and medicine; animal studies show lower glucose and lipids.
cons: Human trials are small; causes wind, loose stools and a maple-like body odour.
cautions: Adds to sugar-lowering medicines; large amounts are avoided in pregnancy.

traditional_use: Classical rasayana fruit, used in Triphala and recorded for prameha.
pros: Common food fruit with a long rasayana record; animal work shows antihyperglycaemic effect.
cons: Human evidence for blood sugar is thin; sour taste; can loosen stools.
cautions: May add to sugar-lowering medicines; a human study shows added antiplatelet effect.
source_note: PMID 21394805 and PMID 19761040 (glycaemic, animal); antiplatelet tag from PMID 24291054, a human study alongside clopidogrel and aspirin

traditional_use: Classical use of haridra for prameha, inflammation and skin disorders.
pros: Everyday kitchen spice; animal and early human work suggests better glucose control.
cons: Curcumin is poorly absorbed alone; evidence is early; can irritate the stomach.
cautions: May slow breakdown of other medicines; a documented interaction with metformin exists.
source_note: PMID 29518605 (curator-confirmed metformin interaction in this project); antiplatelet tag from PMID 16112857 and PMID 20158382

traditional_use: Traditional use of twak as a warming digestive and metabolic spice.
pros: Common spice; a review of randomised trials reports modest falls in blood glucose.
cons: Trial results conflict and the effect is small; cassia types carry a coumarin liver risk.
cautions: Adds to sugar-lowering medicines; true cinnamon is preferred over cassia bark.
source_note: PMID 19930003 (review of randomised controlled trials)

traditional_use: Classical rasayana, guduchi, recorded for prameha and for fevers.
pros: Long classical record; animal studies show lower glucose and better insulin sensitivity.
cons: No good human trials for blood sugar; liver injury has been reported with some products.
cautions: Reported liver injury cases; avoid alongside other medicines that stress the liver.
source_note: PMID 1529024 and PMID 19520137 (glycaemic, animal); the hepatotoxic_risk tag rests on published Indian case series and is general knowledge, not on an abstract in this corpus

traditional_use: Classical use of nimba as a bitter herb for prameha, skin disease and fevers.
pros: Long traditional use; animal work shows the leaf extract lowers blood glucose.
cons: Human evidence is absent; very bitter; the seed oil is toxic, especially to children.
cautions: Adds to sugar-lowering medicines; neem oil must never be given to infants or children.

traditional_use: Traditional use of ghritakumari gel for digestion, skin and metabolic complaints.
pros: A randomised placebo-controlled trial reported lower blood glucose and cholesterol.
cons: One small trial only; the bitter latex is a harsh laxative; gel quality varies widely.
cautions: Laxative latex can lower potassium; the gel adds to sugar-lowering medicines.
source_note: PMID 22198821 (randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in type 2 diabetes)

traditional_use: Traditional use of shigru leaf and pod as food and as a metabolic tonic.
pros: Nutritious leaf eaten as a vegetable; animal studies show better glucose tolerance.
cons: Human evidence is limited; large amounts can loosen the stools.
cautions: May add to both sugar-lowering and blood-pressure-lowering medicines.
source_note: PMID 26124050 and PMID 29175792 (glycaemic); blood-pressure tag from PMID 32412306

traditional_use: Classical use of lashuna as a warming herb for vata and circulatory complaints.
pros: Common food; animal studies report modest falls in blood glucose.
cons: The effect on sugar is small and inconsistent in people; strong smell.
cautions: Raises bleeding risk with blood thinners; a documented warfarin interaction exists.
source_note: PMID 16801983 (glycaemic); warfarin interaction curator-confirmed in this project (PMID 10675182, 19719333, 21919844)

traditional_use: Classical use of Indian snakeroot for raktagata vata and for unmada, mental agitation.
pros: The best known classical Ayurvedic herb for high blood pressure.
cons: Causes marked drowsiness, slow pulse, nasal stuffiness and low mood.
cautions: Avoid if there is depression; adds strongly to blood-pressure and heart-rate-lowering medicines.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Rauvolfia serpentina, plus its well-established pharmacology; this project's abstract corpus holds no study of it

traditional_use: Classical use of arjuna bark for hridroga, the heart-disease group.
pros: Traditional cardiac tonic; animal work supports a cardiovascular effect.
cons: Blood-pressure evidence in people is very limited and indirect.
cautions: May add to the effect of blood-pressure-lowering medicines.

traditional_use: Classical use of punarnava as a diuretic for shotha, fluid swelling.
pros: Long traditional record as a gentle diuretic where fluid is retained.
cons: No human blood-pressure trials; the basis is tradition alone.
cautions: A diuretic effect can disturb fluid and potassium balance alongside heart medicines.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Boerhavia diffusa; this project's abstract corpus holds no cardiovascular study of it

traditional_use: Classical use of lashuna for circulatory complaints.
pros: Food-grade herb; trials and reviews report a small fall in blood pressure.
cons: The fall is modest; smell and stomach upset are common complaints.
cautions: Adds to blood-pressure medicines and raises bleeding risk with blood thinners.
source_note: PMID 11834913 (review of herbs and supplements in cardiovascular disease)

traditional_use: Classical use of jatamansi as a calming herb for the mind and the heart.
pros: Traditional calming herb, used where tension and poor sleep drive blood pressure.
cons: No human blood-pressure evidence; the record is mainly as a sedative.
cautions: Adds to drowsiness from other medicines and may add to blood-pressure lowering.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Nardostachys jatamansi; this project's abstract corpus holds no cardiovascular study of it

traditional_use: Traditional use of shigru as food and as a metabolic tonic.
pros: Edible leaf; animal studies report lower blood pressure in metabolic syndrome models.
cons: No human blood-pressure trials, so the size of any effect is unknown.
cautions: May add to blood-pressure-lowering and sugar-lowering medicines.

traditional_use: Classical use of arjuna bark for hridroga, the heart-disease group.
pros: A small clinical study in heart patients reported less angina and better heart function.
cons: Studies are small, old and unblinded, with no modern confirmation.
cautions: Never a replacement for prescribed heart-failure treatment; may add to blood-pressure lowering.
source_note: PMID 9505018 (patients with post-infarction angina and ischaemic cardiomyopathy)

traditional_use: Classical use of punarnava for shotha, including the swelling of a failing heart.
pros: Traditional diuretic for the leg swelling that accompanies a weak heart.
cons: No clinical trials in heart failure; the basis is tradition alone.
cautions: Diuretic effect can upset potassium and fluid balance, which matters with digoxin.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Boerhavia diffusa in shotha; this project's abstract corpus holds no heart-failure study of it

traditional_use: Classical use of arjuna for hridroga, which includes palpitation.
pros: Traditional cardiac tonic with some human cardiovascular study behind the plant.
cons: Nothing has been studied in atrial fibrillation itself; no rhythm data exist.
cautions: Does not control heart rhythm; an irregular heartbeat needs assessment for stroke risk.
source_note: classical indication hridroga, which covers palpitation; this project's abstract corpus holds no atrial fibrillation study

traditional_use: Classical use of jatamansi for hrit-kampa, palpitation, as a calming cardiac herb.
pros: Traditional calming herb specifically recorded for palpitation.
cons: No human rhythm studies; the evidence is traditional only.
cautions: Does not treat atrial fibrillation or its stroke risk; may add to drowsiness.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Nardostachys jatamansi in hrit-kampa; this project's abstract corpus holds no rhythm study of it

traditional_use: Classical use of lashuna as a warming herb that moves the blood.
pros: Laboratory and animal work shows reduced platelet clumping.
cons: No evidence that it prevents or treats a clot in people.
cautions: Does not replace an anticoagulant; taken with one, bleeding risk rises markedly.
source_note: PMID 11834913 and PMID 13678230 (platelet and antithrombotic activity); warfarin interaction curator-confirmed in this project (PMID 10675182)

traditional_use: Classical use of ardraka for digestion and for vata disorders.
pros: Human platelet studies show gingerols reduce platelet aggregation in the laboratory.
cons: No clinical evidence for preventing or treating a clot.
cautions: Does not replace an anticoagulant and may add to bleeding risk with blood thinners.

traditional_use: Classical use of haridra as an anti-inflammatory herb that moves the blood.
pros: Laboratory work shows curcuminoids inhibit platelet activation.
cons: No clinical clot evidence, and curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own.
cautions: Does not replace an anticoagulant; may add to bleeding risk and slow drug breakdown.

traditional_use: Classical use of arjuna bark for hridroga.
pros: A small study after heart attack reported less angina and better heart function.
cons: Small, old and unblinded, with no data on preventing further heart attacks.
cautions: Not a substitute for prescribed prevention; may add to blood-pressure lowering.

traditional_use: Classical use of lashuna for circulatory complaints.
pros: Reviews report small improvements in blood pressure and in cholesterol.
cons: No proof that it prevents heart attacks or strokes; the effects are modest.
cautions: Raises bleeding risk alongside antiplatelet and anticoagulant medicines.

traditional_use: Classical use of guggulu for medoroga, the fat and lipid disorder group.
pros: Long classical record for lipid disorders, with some older trials of a purified fraction.
cons: Trial results conflict; it can cause rash and stomach upset.
cautions: May speed the breakdown of other medicines and can alter thyroid test results.
source_note: classical Ayurvedic materia medica for Commiphora wightii in medoroga; this project's corpus holds only a multi-herb formulation abstract (PMID 13678230), not a guggul trial

traditional_use: Classical use of haridra as an anti-inflammatory herb.
pros: Kitchen spice; laboratory work supports anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet actions.
cons: No outcome evidence in heart disease, and curcumin is poorly absorbed.
cautions: May add to bleeding risk and slow the breakdown of some heart medicines.
